name: Tooth filing / enamel shaving DIY

lead: This is the practice of abrading or filing one's own teeth at home to even out edges, shorten them or lighten them. The shape change is visible immediately, which is the appeal. A dentist-performed version exists and is called odontoplasty, enameloplasty or contouring.
Abrasive tools physically remove enamel, and because enamel has no cells and does not regrow, the change is permanent. No studies of the DIY version were found.

paras: Forum users describe using a file or sanding tool on small chips, pointed edges or uneven lengths, usually in small touch-ups. People who want a supervised version book a dentist for contouring, which is commonly combined with whitening or bonding.
Dental sources describe permanent enamel loss, possible dentin exposure and greater fracture risk in thinned enamel. No safety data exist for unsupervised home use.

angle.text: Forum users file or sand their own teeth to even out edges, shorten length or lighten shade, and the shape change is visible immediately. Dentists perform a supervised version called contouring. Dentists describe enamel loss as permanent, and no studies of the DIY version exist.

lead: Tooth filing or enamel shaving at home is the practice of using a file, sanding tool or similar abrasive to alter the shape, length or shade of one's own teeth without a dentist. Participants in appearance forums discuss it as a way to even out edges or lighten teeth.

Dentists perform a supervised version called odontoplasty, enameloplasty or contouring, which reshapes teeth by removing part of the enamel.[1] Enamel does not regenerate, so removal is permanent.[2][1]
No studies of do-it-yourself enamel removal were found. This article describes the practice and what dental sources report about enamel and professional contouring, and does not give instructions.

paras: Home enamel removal involves abrasive tools applied to the teeth to change shape, smooth chips, or attempt shade change. Its professional counterpart, odontoplasty, can repair a small chip or alter the length, shape or position of a tooth, and is sometimes described as an alternative to braces in selected cases.[1]

Enamel is about 96 percent mineral and contains no cells, blood vessels or nerves; the cells that formed it are lost before the tooth erupts, so the body cannot regenerate it.[2] Remineralisation can repair some early damage, but dentists cannot restore lost enamel.[2] It is thickest at the cusps, up to about 2.5 mm, and thinner near the gumline.[2] Normal wear is estimated at about 8 micrometres per year.[2]

Dentists who contour teeth note that removal is permanent and may sometimes expose dentin.[1] Dental polishing, a routine office procedure, is reported to remove about one micron of enamel per treatment, a far smaller amount.[3][4]

Dental sources describe loss of enamel and exposure of dentin as risks of enamel removal.[1] Tooth wear literature describes progressive wear exposing dentine, and in severe cases the pulp.[5] Enamel left without dentin underneath is described as more prone to fracture.[2] Because stains inside a tooth originate in dentin or enamel structure, abrasion of the surface does not change intrinsic colour.[6][3]
